subtype: Approach: drawing a sketch before cutting [Action]
passage: In the art room I sit next to Irawati, and this afternoon she had one sheet of thick cardboard, the last in the box. She did not touch the scissors. She drew a windmill on plain paper first, blades, tower, base, with numbers beside each part: 12 cm, 8 cm. Then she cut paper shapes and laid them over the cardboard like a jigsaw. Two blades overlapped, so she moved the tower. Only then did she cut the cardboard, slowly, with no scraps wasted. I would have cut straight away. I cannot say what she felt, but she hummed. - Arnab

qa.q: What did Irawati do before touching the scissors?
qa.a: She drew a windmill on plain paper with numbers beside each part.

qa.q: What might Irawati have been feeling as she worked, and how can Arnab tell?
qa.a: She may have felt calm and focused, since she hummed, though Arnab cannot be sure.

qa.q: What other approach could avoid wasting the cardboard, and why?
qa.a: She could make a full-size mock-up from scrap paper first, so mistakes cost nothing.

qa.q: How does Arnab see Irawati's method compared with Arnab's own?
qa.a: Arnab would have cut straight away, so Arnab finds her method careful and quietly impressive.

grounding: A girl draws a windmill with measurements before cutting, to avoid wasting the only thick sheet of cardboard.

subtype: Approach: drawing a sketch before cutting [Action]
passage:
Monday: Sabina had one sheet of thick cardboard, the back of an old calendar, and a windmill to make for the school fair. Her cousin Sahil said, "Just start cutting." She didn't. On a sheet of newspaper she drew the windmill with numbers: tower 30 cm, four blades of 12 cm, base 15 by 15.
Tuesday: She cut the shapes out of newspaper first and laid them on the cardboard like puzzle pieces. The blades didn't fit beside the tower. She turned them sideways, and everything fitted, with a strip left over for the axle holder.
Friday: At the fair the windmill turned steadily in front of the table fan. Sahil asked if he could borrow her drawing.

qa.q: How tall did Sabina draw the tower?
Why didn't Sabina just start cutting?
qa.a: She felt cautious, worried about wasting her only sheet of thick cardboard.

qa.q: What else could Sabina have tried if the pieces still didn't fit?
qa.a: She could make the blades from thinner card, since not every part needs to be strong, and save the thick sheet for the tower.

qa.q: How does Sahil's view change over the week?
qa.a: At first he says to just start cutting; by Friday he wants to borrow the drawing, so he has come to value the plan.

grounding: Over several days, a girl sketches her windmill with measurements so she does not waste her only thick cardboard.

subtype: Approach: drawing a sketch before cutting [Action]
passage: Harsha, before you cut that chart paper, listen. When your Bhavna-attai was eleven, she wanted to make a windmill for the village science fair. We had only one sheet of thick cardboard, the lid of the box our radio came in. My daughter didn't touch the scissors. She took a pencil and drew the whole windmill on newspaper, with numbers: tower thirty centimetres, blades twelve each, a square base. Then she laid the drawing over the cardboard and frowned. "Appa, the tower and four blades don't fit together." So she rolled the tower from newspaper instead and kept the cardboard for the blades. It won second prize. And the leftover cardboard became her pencil box.

qa.q: What might Bhavna have felt when she frowned at the drawing?
qa.a: She was concerned when she saw the pieces would not fit, then determined to find another way.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story made the biggest difference?
qa.a: Drawing with measurements and laying it over the cardboard, because it showed the problem before a single cut was made.

qa.q: How does the elder remember Bhavna's careful work?
qa.a: With obvious pride, recalling the second prize and even the pencil box made from the leftovers.

grounding: An elder recalls a girl drawing her windmill with measurements to avoid wasting the only thick cardboard.
